summary:
Lesotho does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The common-law offence of sodomy was struck down in 2012, and male same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since; sexual activity between women was never criminalised. A joint stakeholder submission to the Universal Periodic Review filed in October 2024 by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho records same-sex conduct as lawful while documenting the absence of protections.

No general anti-discrimination statute protects LGBTIQ+ people. The Labour Act 2024, the current statutory framework for workplace rights, bans employment discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation and defines workplace gender-based violence and harassment as violence and harassment, including sexual harassment, directed at workers, trainees, probationers, applicants, managers, supervisors, customers, clients, suppliers or contractors because of sex, gender or gender identity, or affecting persons of a particular sex, gender or gender identity disproportionately. The Act operates in the employment sphere only.

No law in Lesotho permits a change of legal gender marker on documents. A 2017 constitutional analysis by the Southern African Litigation Centre argues that section 4(1) of the Constitution, in its references to sex and other status, should be read to include gender identity in line with the UN Human Rights Committee, and warns that a transgender person travelling on a passport whose gender marker does not match their presentation could face charges. A October 2020 briefing by the Southern African Litigation Centre, the People's Matrix Association and the Women in Law Southern Africa Lesotho office benchmarks Lesotho's law and policy against international best practice and identifies the Matrix as the only known LGBTI organisation in the country.

The October 2024 joint stakeholder submission documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and SOGIESC discrimination at community level. A November 2024 submission by the International Commission of Jurists to the same review places LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination among three key concerns, alongside inclusive education for children with disabilities and the revocation of practising certificates held by NGO lawyers.

On partner recognition, the Marriage Act No. 10 of 1974 and customary law permit marriage only between opposite-sex couples, and same-sex marriages and civil unions are not recognised. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under the sex recorded at their birth has no recognised union in Lesotho.

On enforcement, the 2016 United States Department of State human rights report for Lesotho stated that LGBTI persons faced societal discrimination and official insensitivity, that same-sex relationships were taboo and not openly discussed, and that no assaults were reported because incidents often went unreported for fear of stigma. The same report recorded that the Matrix Support Group operated freely in all ten districts with a good working relationship with the Lesotho Mounted Police Service, including police intervention in December 2015 to enable a lesbian forced from home by her brothers to return, and a supportive police escort for a march of approximately 200 people in Maseru on 21 May 2016. The most recent documented instance of violence against LGBT people in this record is the October 2024 Universal Periodic Review submission, which records rape and assault; no later instance is documented.

Support structures exist. The Matrix Support Group was established in 2009 and fully registered in 2010 as an LGBTI organisation including transgender and intersex people, working principally through engagement with partner organisations on gender-based violence. It organised the first gay pride march on 18 May 2013 in central Maseru with supportive authorities providing an escort, and pride marches have been held annually since, attracting a few hundred people.
tangentialFactors:
In June 2016, after the UN General Assembly High-Level Meeting on HIV/AIDS, Deputy Prime Minister Mothetjoa Metsing stated that the government would look into decriminalising same-sex relationships in order to stop the spread of HIV. The statement indicates an official framing of same-sex conduct as a public-health question at that date.

Health-service context is shaped by HIV prevalence: a source in this inventory describes Lesotho as having the second highest HIV prevalence in the world, at reportedly 25 percent of residents infected, and records LGBTI activists reaching out to HIV-positive people with prevention strategies. This figure is country-wide rather than trans-specific.

The International Commission of Jurists submission of November 2024 raises two concerns unrelated to LGBTIQ+ rights alongside it: inclusive education for children with disabilities and the revocation of practising certificates held by lawyers working with NGOs. The presence of the second concern in the same submission indicates pressure on the domestic legal-aid space in which LGBTI litigation is brought.

The Southern African Litigation Centre's 2017 finding that the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omitted gender and sexual orientation predates the Labour Act 2024, which adds sexual orientation in employment. The record therefore shows a change in the employment layer between 2017 and 2024, while the constitutional and gender-recognition questions raised in 2017 remain without a documented statutory answer.
localsOnly:
Section 127(4) of the Children's Protection and Welfare Act 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination based on sexual orientation in the selection of a diversion programme, process or option, and requires equal access for all children. This is a child-justice provision and does not extend to adult proceedings.

Under the Child Welfare and Protection Act of 2011, only married couples of opposite sexes may adopt jointly; single men and same-sex couples are not permitted to adopt.

Since 2013 the Credit Reporting Regulations have provided that credit information relating to sexual orientation may not be contained in credit bureau records, except to the extent it is self-evident from the marital status and family member list.

The National Identity Cards Act 9 of 2011 governs national identity cards. Section 8(1) provides that the Director shall take reasonable practicable steps to ensure that personal information entered into the Register is complete, accurate and updated where necessary. A secondary source in this inventory interprets that provision as potentially allowing transgender people to change their legal gender on identity documents.

The Matrix Support Group, established in 2009 and registered in 2010, is the principal resident-facing LGBTI organisation, including transgender and intersex members, and works on gender-based violence with partner organisations. It has run public outreach through film screenings, radio programmes, public gatherings, social media and an electronic billboard in central Maseru, and pride marches have been held annually in the capital since 18 May 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no procedure, eligibility criteria, penalties or recorded instances of a granted legal gender change are documented anywhere in the inventory. The only relevant provision identified is section 8(1) of the National Identity Cards Act 9 of 2011, and the reading of that section as permitting a gender change is asserted by a secondary source rather than by regulation or case law.

Unresolved: the sources state that there are no transgender-specific provisions on airport or border screening, sex-segregated facilities, custody, detention or gender-affirming care. The absence of a sourced provision is not a finding that no differential treatment occurs.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory makes any documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically. The only tolerance statement available is LGBTI-general, namely that attitudes towards members of the LGBTI community are slowly evolving and becoming more tolerant and accepting.

Unresolved: whether the Labour Act 2024's employment non-discrimination ban extends to gender identity, beyond the gender-based-violence definition that names gender identity, is not stated in the sources.

Unresolved: the sources conflict on the state of the criminal law. The 2016 United States Department of State report stated that the law at that time prohibited consensual sexual relations between men but that authorities did not enforce it, while other sources in the inventory record the common-law offence as struck down in 2012. No court record reconciling the two accounts is present.

Unresolved: the 2017 warning that a transgender person with a non-matching passport marker could be charged cites no statute, charge or decided case.
